question: Can you explain what periodization means in athletic training and why a coach would use it?
lookingFor: Working understanding of macro/meso/microcycles and why varying load and intensity over a season prevents plateaus and injury.

bullets: Define periodization as structured variation of volume and intensity over time
Mention distinct phases such as base, build, and taper, and their purpose
Link it to preventing overtraining and peaking for competition
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Periodization is basically the deliberate planning of training over weeks and months so that an athlete peaks at the right moment rather than just training hard all year round. You typically break a season into phases, a base phase to build general fitness, a build phase where intensity climbs and volume drops, and a taper before the key competition so the athlete arrives fresh. I got interested in this after watching a local swim club's coach adjust sessions week to week, and I read that without it athletes are far more likely to plateau or get injured from constantly training at the same high intensity.

commonMistakes: Describing periodization as just 'training hard then resting'
No mention of distinct phases
Confusing periodization with a single week's schedule
followUps: How might periodization differ for a youth athlete compared to an elite adult?

question: The '10,000 hours' idea is widely quoted in coaching. What does the evidence actually say about deliberate practice and sporting expertise?
lookingFor: Willingness to interrogate a popular claim against real evidence, rather than repeat it as settled fact.

bullets: Explain that the original research came from music and was popularised well beyond what it showed
Cite that meta-analyses find practice explains only a modest share of the variance in sporting performance, often around a fifth
Identify the other contributors — training quality, coaching, genetics, starting age, and the sampling of multiple sports early on
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It gets quoted as though it were a law, but the original work was on violinists and it reported an average, not a threshold anybody has to cross. When people have gone back and looked at sport specifically, accumulated practice tends to explain something like a fifth of the variance in performance, which is real but nowhere near the whole story. What fills the rest is the quality of the practice rather than the hours, plus coaching, physiology, and when someone started. I find the more interesting question is what makes an hour of practice count, because that is the part a coach can actually influence.

commonMistakes: Repeating the 10,000-hour figure as established fact
Swinging to the opposite extreme and claiming talent is everything
Confusing total time spent training with deliberate practice
followUps: If practice quality matters more than quantity, how would you design a session to maximise it?

question: What's the difference between functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome, and how would a coach tell them apart?
lookingFor: Nuanced grasp distinguishing planned short-term fatigue from a maladaptive state, with practical monitoring.

bullets: Define overreaching as planned, short-term fatigue that recovers with supercompensation
Define overtraining syndrome as prolonged and maladaptive, involving mood and hormonal disturbance
Mention monitoring tools coaches use such as mood questionnaires, resting heart rate, and performance trends
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Functional overreaching is when a coach deliberately pushes an athlete into a short period of fatigue and reduced performance, knowing that a few days or a couple of weeks of recovery afterward will produce a rebound, a supercompensation, so it's actually a planned tool. Overtraining syndrome is what happens when that fatigue isn't allowed to resolve, so it drags on for months, comes with mood disturbance, poor sleep, and a performance drop that doesn't bounce back with normal rest. The tricky part for a coach is that early overreaching and early overtraining look almost identical day to day, so you need to track things like resting heart rate, mood questionnaires, and performance trends over weeks, not just how one session went.

commonMistakes: Treating the two as the same thing
No mention of a time-based distinction
No practical monitoring method offered
followUps: What would you do if you suspected an athlete was heading toward overtraining but they insisted they were fine?

question: What's the difference between implicit and explicit approaches to teaching a motor skill, and when might a coach choose one over the other?
lookingFor: Understanding of instructional theory and situational judgement about when each approach fits.

bullets: Define explicit learning as rule-based, verbal instruction the athlete can consciously describe
Define implicit learning as skill acquired through guided discovery or constraints with little conscious rule-recall
Give a situational reason to favour one, such as implicit under pressure or explicit for beginners needing safety
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Explicit learning is when you give an athlete clear verbal rules, like telling a beginner golfer exactly where to place their hands, and they can consciously recall and apply those instructions. Implicit learning happens more through guided practice and changing the constraints of a drill, so the athlete picks up the skill without being able to fully explain the rule they're following. I understand implicit methods tend to hold up better under pressure because there are fewer conscious rules to choke on, which is why some coaches use constraint-based games for experienced players, but for a complete beginner you probably need some explicit instruction just for safety and basic technique.

commonMistakes: Confusing implicit with 'no coaching at all'
No mention of pressure or choking research
Unable to give a concrete example of either method
followUps: Can you think of a drill that teaches a skill implicitly?

question: Talent identification programmes try to spot future elite athletes early. What are the limitations of trying to predict adult sporting success from a child's performance?
lookingFor: Critical, evidence-aware reasoning rather than blind faith in early testing.

bullets: Note the relative age effect and maturational timing distort early performance
Mention that early physical dominance doesn't reliably predict adult skill or motivation
Suggest a more cautious, broad-based alternative approach
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of what looks like talent in a ten or eleven year old is really just who happened to be born earlier in the selection year or who hit puberty sooner, so you end up selecting for maturity rather than underlying ability, that's the relative age effect. Research also shows a lot of kids who dominate at twelve don't make it as seniors, and plenty who weren't picked out early do, because things like motivation, coachability, and how a late developer eventually matches up physically matter just as much. I think that's a real argument for keeping talent pathways broad and reassessing regularly rather than locking a child into or out of a programme based on one early assessment.

commonMistakes: Assuming early standout performance reliably predicts adult success
No mention of relative age effect or biological maturation
Offering no alternative or caveat
followUps: How would you design a fairer talent pathway given these limitations?

question: What's the difference between a task-involving and an ego-involving motivational climate, and why might it matter for a young athlete?
lookingFor: Applied understanding of achievement goal theory and its link to real outcomes.

bullets: Define task climate as effort, improvement, and mastery focused
Define ego climate as outcome, comparison, and winning focused
Link the distinction to outcomes like enjoyment, dropout, or anxiety
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A task-involving climate is one where a coach praises effort, personal improvement, and trying new things, so success is measured against your own progress. An ego-involving climate is more about winning and being better than teammates, where mistakes are punished and comparison is constant. From what I've read and seen in my own club, a task climate tends to keep young athletes enjoying the sport longer and coping better with setbacks, while a heavily ego climate is linked to higher dropout and anxiety, even though it can look effective in the very short term.

commonMistakes: Saying ego climate is simply 'bad coaching' with no nuance
No link to real outcomes like dropout or anxiety
Confusing the two terms
followUps: Can a coach blend both without harming athletes?

question: What practical things can a coach do to build an athlete's self-efficacy, their belief they can succeed at a specific task?
lookingFor: Application of psychology, such as mastery experiences and modelling, beyond generic 'be positive' answers.

bullets: Reference sources like mastery experiences, modelling, and verbal persuasion
Give a concrete coaching example
Show understanding that generic praise alone is weak
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Self-efficacy is built most strongly through actual mastery experiences, so a coach breaking a hard skill into smaller wins an athlete can genuinely achieve does more than any pep talk. Watching a similar peer succeed, what's called modelling, also helps, which is why pairing a nervous athlete with someone slightly ahead of them can work well. Verbal encouragement matters too but it's the weakest of the sources on its own, so I'd want to combine it with structured, achievable challenges rather than just telling someone 'you've got this'.

commonMistakes: Reducing the whole idea to 'positive encouragement'
No mention of mastery experiences or modelling
No concrete coaching example
followUps: How would you rebuild confidence in an athlete coming back from a bad injury?

question: Can you explain the force-velocity relationship in muscle contraction and why it matters for designing strength training?
lookingFor: Genuine subject depth in exercise science and biomechanics, with a training application.

bullets: State the inverse relationship between contraction velocity and maximal force capacity
Link to training implications, heavy slow lifts for max force, light fast lifts for speed
Mention power as the balance point coaches often train for
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The force-velocity relationship describes how a muscle can produce its highest force only when contracting slowly, and as the speed of contraction increases the maximum force it can generate drops off. Practically that means very heavy, slow lifting mainly develops maximal strength, while lighter, fast movements like jump training develop speed, and neither on its own necessarily improves power, which sits in the middle of that curve. That's why a lot of strength programmes for sports use a mix, heavy lifts alongside plyometrics, to try to shift the whole curve rather than just one end of it.

commonMistakes: Only knowing that 'heavy weights build strength' with no curve concept
Confusing force-velocity with simple fatigue
No training application given
followUps: How would you programme training differently for a sprinter versus a powerlifter given this relationship?

subtopic: Suspecting doping in an athlete you coach
question: As a coach you notice sudden, unexplained gains in one of your athletes and suspect possible doping. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning balancing duty of care, evidence, and fairness, not a snap accusation.

bullets: Acknowledge you can't accuse without evidence but can't ignore the concern either
Describe a private conversation first, framed around welfare rather than accusation
Escalate through proper channels if concern persists, prioritising health and sport integrity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't jump straight to an accusation because sudden gains can have innocent explanations, a growth spurt, a new training block, better sleep, but I also couldn't just ignore it. I'd start with a private, non-confrontational conversation, asking genuinely how training has been going and being honest that I've noticed a big change, which gives them a chance to explain or to talk to me if something is wrong. If my concern didn't go away after that, I think I'd have an obligation to raise it through whatever proper reporting channel the organisation has, because doping isn't just a personal choice, it's unfair to everyone else competing clean and it can seriously harm the athlete's health.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to a public accusation with no evidence
Deciding to say nothing at all to avoid conflict
Framing it purely as rule-breaking with no concern for the athlete's wellbeing
followUps: What if the athlete is a minor and you suspect a parent is involved?

subtopic: Parental pressure on a young athlete
question: You coach a talented twelve-year-old whose parent pushes them to train far beyond what you think is healthy. How do you handle this?
lookingFor: Safeguarding awareness balanced with respect for the parental role, and sound escalation judgement.

bullets: Prioritise the child's physical and psychological welfare as the deciding factor
Describe talking to the parent directly with evidence and rationale before escalating
Know when and how to involve club safeguarding structures if it continues
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first responsibility is the child's wellbeing, not the parent's ambitions, so if I genuinely thought the training load was risking injury or burnout I'd need to act rather than just go along with it. I'd start by talking to the parent directly, explaining specifically what I'm seeing, like signs of fatigue or the child losing enjoyment, and try to agree a more sustainable plan together, since most parents want what's best even if they're pushing too hard. If that conversation didn't change anything and I still had real concerns about the child's welfare, I'd raise it with the club's safeguarding lead, because at that point it's not just a coaching disagreement anymore.

commonMistakes: Avoiding the conflict and quietly going along with the parent's demands
Escalating immediately without first speaking to the parent
Framing it only as a performance issue rather than a welfare one
followUps: What signs would actually tell you the child is at risk, rather than just working hard?

subtopic: Dropping a star player for the team's sake
question: Your most talented player has been disruptive to team morale. Do you drop them for a big upcoming match, even though it likely costs you the win?
lookingFor: Weighing short-term performance against long-term team culture, with willingness to make an unpopular call.

bullets: Recognise the genuine tension between winning and team culture or fairness
Consider whether the behaviour was addressed directly before jumping to dropping them
Land on a defensible decision with reasoning, not indecision
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to have already had a direct conversation with them about the impact of their behaviour before it ever got to matchday, because dropping someone should never be the first response. But if the disruption continued and I genuinely believed it was damaging the team more than their individual quality was adding, I think I'd have to drop them, even for a big match, because a coach who lets one player undermine the group loses the trust of everyone else on the team. Winning one match isn't worth what it would cost me if the rest of the squad felt the rules didn't apply to the best player.

commonMistakes: Refusing to commit to a decision either way
Ignoring the team culture cost entirely in favour of winning
No mention of addressing the behaviour before punishment
followUps: How would you communicate that decision to the player and to the rest of the team?

subtopic: Data and wearable tech in coaching
question: Many teams now use GPS trackers and wearables to monitor athlete load. What's your view on the benefits and risks of relying heavily on this data?
lookingFor: Balanced, informed awareness of a live debate in the field, not blind enthusiasm for technology.

bullets: Note the benefit of objective load monitoring and individualised training
Note the risk of data overload and over-reliance replacing a coach's judgement
Land on a balanced view of data as a tool, not a replacement for judgement
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: GPS and wearable data let a coach see things you can't judge by eye, like exact distance covered at high speed or how quickly an athlete's heart rate recovers between efforts, which is genuinely useful for spotting injury risk before it becomes a problem. But I think there's a real risk of coaches leaning on the numbers so much that they stop trusting what the athlete is actually telling them or what the coach can see with their own eyes, and constant monitoring can also add pressure, some athletes have said it makes them feel watched rather than supported. My view is the data should sit alongside a coach's judgement and the athlete's own feedback, not replace either of them.

commonMistakes: Uncritical enthusiasm with no downside mentioned
Dismissing data entirely as unnecessary
No specific example of what the data measures
followUps: How would you handle an athlete who becomes anxious about their tracked numbers?

question: There's ongoing debate about transgender athletes competing in female categories. How would you, as a coach, think through this issue?
lookingFor: Mature, respectful engagement with a genuinely contested policy debate, avoiding glib certainty.

bullets: Acknowledge the debate involves a real tension between inclusion and competitive fairness
Show awareness that governing bodies differ and the science and policy are still evolving
Focus on treating athletes with respect while following the sport's current rules
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think this is genuinely one of the harder issues in sport right now because it sits at a real tension between including trans athletes fairly and making sure competition stays fair for other athletes in the category, and reasonable, well-informed people land in different places on it. Different governing bodies have taken different approaches and the science on things like retained physical advantage after transition is still being actively researched and debated, so I don't think it's my place to pretend there's an easy answer. As a coach, what I can control is following whatever policy my sport's governing body sets, and treating every athlete in my care with respect regardless of where they land in that debate.

commonMistakes: Stating a strong personal policy opinion as if it were settled fact
Dismissing the issue as unimportant or refusing to engage at all
Being disrespectful toward either side of the debate
followUps: How would you support a trans athlete on your own team amid that wider debate?

question: There's an ongoing debate about whether young athletes should specialise in one sport early or sample several. Where do you stand, and why?
lookingFor: Awareness of current sports science consensus paired with a reasoned personal position.

bullets: Show awareness that most evidence favours sampling multiple sports before adolescence
Note exceptions where early specialization is arguably necessary, such as gymnastics
Give a reasoned personal stance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Most of the research I've come across favours sampling several sports through childhood, because it builds broader motor skills, seems to lower injury and burnout risk, and kids who sample often still reach elite level later, just via a different route. There are exceptions, sports like gymnastics or figure skating where peak performance windows are so early that some specialization seems almost necessary, so I don't think it's an absolute rule. My own view leans toward sampling being the safer default, with specialization becoming reasonable once a young athlete themselves, not just a parent or coach, clearly wants to commit.

commonMistakes: Stating an opinion with no reference to actual evidence
Treating it as a rule with no exceptions
Confusing specialization with simply 'training hard'
followUps: How would you handle a young athlete who wants to specialise early against your advice?

question: In recent years several high-profile athletes have spoken openly about mental health struggles under competitive pressure. What does that mean for how coaches should operate?
lookingFor: Awareness of a genuine cultural shift in sport and its practical implications for coaching practice.

bullets: Reference the broader shift toward athletes speaking openly and sport bodies responding
Identify a practical implication for coaching practice, such as checking in beyond performance
Avoid overclaiming clinical expertise the coach doesn't have
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's a really positive shift that elite athletes have felt able to speak publicly about mental health, because it's pushed governing bodies and coaches to stop treating performance and wellbeing as separate things. Practically, for me as a coach it means regularly checking in on how an athlete is doing as a person, not just their split times or stats, and creating an environment where saying 'I'm struggling' doesn't feel like admitting weakness. I'd also want to know exactly who to refer someone to, a sports psychologist or the club's welfare officer, because I know my job is to notice and support, not to try to diagnose or treat something myself.

commonMistakes: Suggesting the coach should act as a therapist
Treating it as irrelevant to their own coaching practice
No mention of a specific referral pathway
followUps: What would you actually say to an athlete who told you they were struggling before a big competition?

question: Youth and college sport is becoming increasingly commercialised, with debates about paying young athletes or letting them profit from their name. What's your take?
lookingFor: Informed awareness of a live governance debate paired with a reasoned view.

bullets: Show awareness of the shift toward athletes earning from sponsorship and their own name
Weigh the fairness argument against the risk of distorting development-stage decisions
Land on a considered position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's a real shift happening where young or student athletes can now earn from sponsorship and their own name in a way that wasn't allowed a decade ago, and I understand the argument, they're generating real commercial value and audiences, so it seems fair they can benefit from it too. My concern is that money entering the picture that early can distort decision-making, like a young athlete or their family choosing a programme or specialising based on sponsorship potential rather than what's actually best for their development. I think some framework that lets athletes benefit without it overtaking development-stage decisions is the right balance, though I don't think anyone has fully solved that yet.

commonMistakes: No awareness the debate exists at all
One-sided view with no acknowledgment of the development risk
Confusing this with professional athlete salaries generally
followUps: Would your view change for a fourteen-year-old versus an eighteen-year-old?

subtopic: Athlete pushes back on your plan
question: An athlete you coach flatly refuses to follow the training plan you've set, insisting their old approach worked better. What do you do?
lookingFor: Collaborative problem-solving over pure authority, and willingness to listen and adapt.

bullets: Start by genuinely listening to why they disagree rather than asserting authority
Look for evidence or a trial period rather than a flat standoff
Show willingness to adjust if they raise a legitimate point, while explaining your reasoning clearly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to actually understand why they preferred their old approach before assuming I'm simply right, because sometimes an athlete's instinct about their own body is picking up on something real. I'd explain my reasoning behind the new plan clearly, what problem it's meant to solve, and then suggest we trial it for a few weeks with a way to measure whether it's working, rather than just insisting on it. If it turned out their concern was valid, I'd genuinely adjust the plan, because good coaching isn't about winning the argument, it's about finding what actually helps them improve.

commonMistakes: Simply asserting authority with 'because I said so'
Caving immediately with no attempt to explain the reasoning
No concrete plan for resolving the disagreement
followUps: What if they still refused after that conversation?

question: Your team has lost four matches in a row and you can see morale dropping fast. What would you actually do in that week's training?
lookingFor: Practical, psychologically informed response rather than vague reassurance.

bullets: Diagnose whether the issue is skill, fatigue, or confidence before reacting
Describe a concrete adjustment, such as shifting focus to controllable process goals
Balance honesty about the run with rebuilding belief
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: First I'd want to work out what's actually driving the slump, whether it's genuine fatigue, a tactical issue, or just confidence collapsing after a few losses, because the fix is different for each. If it looked like a confidence problem, which is common after a losing streak, I'd probably shift that week's training toward things we can control and clearly succeed at, smaller technical wins and process goals rather than results, to rebuild some belief before the next match. I'd also be honest with the team that the run is real and it matters, because pretending everything's fine usually reads as dishonest and makes things worse, not better.

commonMistakes: Generic 'stay positive' answer with no concrete action
Ignoring the need to diagnose the actual cause first
Either denying the problem or being harshly critical with no rebuilding plan
followUps: How would you handle a senior player who's publicly criticising your decisions during this run?

subtopic: Injured key athlete before a championship
question: Your best athlete is carrying a minor injury just before the championship. They insist they're fine to play, but you're not fully sure. What do you do?
lookingFor: Prioritising long-term health over short-term result, with appropriate use of medical judgement.

bullets: Refuse to rely on the athlete's own assurance alone; defer to appropriate medical assessment
Weigh short-term competitive gain against the risk of worsening the injury
Make and own a clear decision rather than passing responsibility entirely to the athlete
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't take the athlete's word alone as enough, however much they want to play, because an athlete under pressure to compete is rarely the most objective judge of their own injury, so I'd want a proper medical or physio assessment before deciding anything. If the medical advice was that playing carried a real risk of making the injury worse, I'd have to make the harder call and hold them out, even for a championship, because a short-term result isn't worth risking a longer-term injury that could cost them far more. I think part of being a good coach is being willing to be the person who says no when the athlete themselves can't be objective.

commonMistakes: Deferring the whole decision to the athlete's own wishes
No mention of getting a proper medical opinion
Framing it purely as a performance trade-off with no health consideration
followUps: What would you say to the athlete if they were angry about being held out?

subtopic: Choosing between two equally matched athletes
question: Two athletes are genuinely equal in ability but there's only one spot on the team for a big event. How would you decide, and how would you handle telling the one who misses out?
lookingFor: Fair, transparent decision process combined with empathetic but honest communication.

bullets: Identify a legitimate tie-breaking factor beyond raw ability, such as recent form or role fit
Commit to a transparent process communicated in advance, not an arbitrary gut call
Describe delivering the news honestly and respectfully, with a path forward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If two athletes are truly equal on ability, I'd look for a legitimate factor beyond that, like who's shown better form in the most recent weeks, or who fits a specific tactical need for that event, and I'd want that criteria to be something I'd explained to the squad in advance, not something I invent afterward to justify a gut feeling. When I told the athlete who missed out, I'd be honest about exactly why, rather than being vague to spare their feelings, because vague reasons are actually harder to accept than a clear one. I'd also make clear what they'd need to show me to get the nod next time, so it's not just a closed door.

commonMistakes: Refusing to actually name a decision criterion
Being vague or evasive when delivering the bad news
No forward-looking path offered to the athlete who missed out
followUps: What if the athlete who missed out accused you of favouritism?

question: How would you expect a periodized training plan for a fourteen-year-old to differ from one for an adult elite athlete in the same sport?
lookingFor: Ability to apply periodization theory in light of growth and maturation, not just repeat adult templates.

bullets: Note lower absolute intensity and volume with more emphasis on general athletic development
Account for growth spurts and biological maturation affecting load tolerance and coordination
Emphasise long-term development goals over short-term peaking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For a fourteen-year-old I'd expect far less emphasis on peaking for one specific competition and far more on general athletic development, movement skill, coordination, and controlled exposure to different training stimuli, because their body is still growing and adapting in ways an adult's isn't. Growth spurts in particular can temporarily affect coordination and increase injury risk, so load needs to be more conservative and flexible around that, rather than locked into a rigid adult-style peak. Ultimately the goal at that age isn't maximum performance this season, it's building a foundation that lets them handle serious adult-level training later without breaking down.

commonMistakes: Simply scaling down an adult plan by reducing numbers
No mention of growth or maturation effects
Focusing on short-term peaking rather than long-term development
followUps: How would you monitor a growth spurt's effect on an athlete's training tolerance?

question: What signs would make you suspect an athlete is heading toward burnout, and how would you respond?
lookingFor: Practical recognition of warning signs plus a sensible, welfare-first response.

bullets: Name concrete signs such as declining performance despite effort, reduced enjoyment, and withdrawal
Distinguish burnout from simple tiredness by its persistence and emotional component
Describe a response focused on reducing load and an honest conversation, not pushing through
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd be looking for things like performance dropping even though the athlete is still putting in effort, them seeming flat or withdrawn around training rather than their usual self, and a loss of the enjoyment that used to be obvious, not just one bad week but a pattern over several. What separates that from normal tiredness is the emotional piece, burnout tends to come with a real loss of motivation and sometimes irritability, not just physical fatigue. If I saw that pattern, I'd want to have an honest, low-pressure conversation with them fairly quickly and look at genuinely reducing their load rather than just telling them to push through, because pushing through is usually exactly what got them there.

commonMistakes: Confusing normal tiredness with burnout
No concrete signs given, just a vague 'I'd notice'
Response is to push harder rather than reduce load
followUps: How would you tell the difference between burnout and a genuine motivation problem?

question: What are the benefits and limitations of using video analysis to give athletes feedback on technique?
lookingFor: Balanced, applied understanding of a common coaching tool and its pitfalls.

bullets: Benefit: objective record the athlete can see, useful for fast or complex movements
Limitation: risk of overloading a beginner with information
Show judgement about timing feedback so it doesn't undermine performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Video gives you an objective record an athlete can actually see for themselves, which is really valuable for fast or complex movements where they genuinely can't feel what their body is doing in the moment, like a swimmer's stroke or a sprinter's start. The limitation is that showing someone too much detail at once, especially a beginner, can overload them and actually make their technique worse because they start over-thinking simple movements. I'd want to be selective, picking one or two key points to show rather than a full breakdown, and timing it so it doesn't interrupt the flow of a session, straight after a competition is often not the moment either.

commonMistakes: Treating video as an unqualified good with no downside
No mention of information overload risk for beginners
No thought given to timing of feedback
followUps: How would feedback change for an eight-year-old compared to an experienced adult athlete?

question: Coaching for disability or Para-sport has grown significantly. What do you think a mainstream coach needs to understand to coach inclusively?
lookingFor: Genuine awareness that inclusive coaching requires real, athlete-specific adaptation, not token gestures.

bullets: Recognise that individual variation within a classification means adaptation is athlete-specific
Show awareness this is a growing, professionalising area with proper classification systems
Emphasise listening to the athlete about what they actually need
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the key thing is that disability sport isn't one category, athletes within the same classification can still need really different adaptations, so a coach can't just apply a single template and assume it covers everyone. It's also become a much more professionalised and structured part of coaching, with proper classification systems and dedicated Para-pathways, so it deserves the same serious technical attention as any other coaching specialism, not a token afterthought. Practically I think the most important thing is actually asking the athlete what works for them and listening properly, because they usually know their own body and what adaptations help far better than I would guess.

commonMistakes: Treating disability sport as a single uniform category
Treating it as a minor add-on rather than a serious coaching specialism
Assuming rather than asking the athlete what adaptations they need
followUps: How would you adapt a drill you already use for a mainstream group to make it inclusive?

question: A parent asks you to advise their fifteen-year-old on taking a legal performance supplement to help them make the team. What's your view?
lookingFor: Cautious, welfare-first reasoning about a genuinely grey ethical area, with awareness of the limits of a coach's expertise.

bullets: Distinguish legality from appropriateness for a still-developing young athlete
Recognise the limits of a coach's own expertise and the need for qualified medical advice
Consider the message it sends about relying on supplements over training fundamentals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Something being legal doesn't automatically make it appropriate for a fifteen-year-old whose body is still developing, so my instinct would be caution rather than a quick yes. I'd also be honest that advising on supplements really isn't within a coach's expertise, so I'd want to direct the family to a qualified sports nutritionist or doctor rather than giving an opinion I'm not qualified to give. Beyond the safety question, I'd also gently push back on the underlying idea, at fifteen I think training fundamentals, sleep, and nutrition basics matter far more than any supplement, and I wouldn't want a young athlete or their parent thinking a supplement is a shortcut past that.

commonMistakes: Giving a confident personal recommendation despite lacking the expertise
Assuming legal automatically means safe or appropriate for a minor
Dismissing the parent's concern instead of engaging with it constructively
followUps: How would you respond if the parent pushed back, saying 'but it's legal, what's the harm'?
